newsitem.title: UK: British bonds ruffled by election, rate concern.
newsitem.headline: British bonds ruffled by election, rate concern.

text.p: Vows by Britain's opposition Labour Party not to raise income tax rates if it wins the next election seem too good to be true, leaving bond investors fretting over how it might meet that promise, analysts said on Tuesday.
The uncertainty, combined with a cloudy interest rate picture, will keep British government bonds confined to a corner against other government debt until after the election, due by May, they said.
"If Labour intends to keep income tax rates the same, they should be clearer on how plans are going to be funded," said Phil Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC James Capel.

"That is really the big concern for the market," he said. "What we'll see is the spread becoming expensive at levels close of 175-180 basis points over Bunds and looking cheap around 200 basis points."
By midsession the yield spread of 10-year benchmark gilts over German Bunds was quoted at 179 basis points or 1.79 percentage points.

Labour's finance spokesman, Gordon Brown, pledged on Monday not to raise the standard or top rates of income tax if his party wins the election. He also vowed to stick to the present Conservative government's public spending targets in its first two years in office.
The plans were bold and broke with the historic Party line of using taxes to fund public programmes. But far from being reassured, gilts were left on edge, analysts said.
"The message from Mr Brown was so restrictive that I think the market just doesn't believe it will happen," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Investment Bank here.
"Labour is so worried about the legacy of the 1992 election when they announced all of those (planned) tax increases, they have gone in the opposite direction," Coleman said.
This time around, the market was left wondering where the money for public services would come from, analysts said.

Restricting income tax relief, such as the married couples allowance and tax-free pension savings, are obvious choices. Raising corporate taxes and national insurance contributions are other avenues left open, analysts said.
"I don't see any reason why they can't stick to the spending freeze but I think it will imply back-door tax hikes," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets.
Analysts said short-term pressures such as December retail sales news on Wednesday and supply concerns will push the gilt/Bund spread to the wider end of the range in the near term.
Then there is the question of interest rates.

Bank of England Governor Eddie George called for a "modest pre-emptive" tightening of fiscal policy in a speech to bankers in Edinburgh on Monday night. He also said the strength of the pound should not be used as an excuse to delay a rise.
"What George is saying is not particularly new. We know the bank favours an early rate rise and does not see strong sterling as a reason for preventing any tightening," said HSBC's Tyson.

Although recent data shows inflation remains subdued, growth remains strong and the market will be on alert for a rate rise after the February 5 monetary meeting between George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

"The market profile has got to be that we go out to 200 basis points (on the gilt/Bund spread) on a combination of upbeat consumption numbers, the implications for inflation and a base rate hike and the politics," said Roberts at NatWest.

But beyond the election there is potential for gilts to get their own back against other European bonds, against which they have been underperforming as attention focused on those countries clearly aiming for European Economic and Monetary Union.
Policy was likely to remain much the same, soothing market fears about a tax-and-spend Labour government, analysts said.

"There will be a period of catchup when yield-hungry investors will suddenly look at the gilt market and see the pick-up they can get on yields and spreads will come racing in," said Roberts, targeting 100 basis points on the gilt/Bund spread by the second half of the year.
